videoIdeas.title: Why young Muslims can't hold a conversation anymore
videoIdeas.hook: The amount of you that can't string a sentence together in a room full of people is embarrassing — and it's not your fault, but it is your problem.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your own post on this exact topic (DbilFRjsJ3v) pulled 617 views with 0 comments — the idea has legs but the delivery was flat and had no hook. Doctordaanish and saffanabanana are winning right now with blunt, direct 'you're doing this wrong' openers. This reworks your own proven subject with a sharper hook and an actual takeaway.
videoIdeas.script: The amount of you that can't hold a conversation in a room full of people is embarrassing. And it's not fully your fault — you grew up texting instead of talking. But it's still your problem. Here's the thing nobody tells you: public speaking isn't a talent, it's a rep. You're not bad at speaking, you're just unpracticed. You avoid the small conversations — the shopkeeper, the uncle at the masjid, the person next to you — and then wonder why you freeze when it actually matters. Start small. Speak to one stranger a day. Say the thing out loud before you overthink it. Your tongue is a muscle. Train it, or stay quiet your whole life and call it shyness.

visuals.setting: Filmed outdoors near a busy high street or masjid entrance, natural daylight, plain fitted top. Standing, slightly higher energy, talking straight to camera like you're pulling someone aside.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'You can't talk to people. Let's fix it.' appears over you standing silent for a beat in a crowd before you start speaking — the contrast of a loud environment and you calm sells it.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence: start on 'And it's still your problem —' then cut back to the real first line
Pattern interrupt: hold up your phone, then put it face-down on a table before speaking
On-screen text punchline that stays: 'Shyness is just avoidance with a nicer name'

videoIdeas.title: Leadership is competence AND trust — not just vibes
videoIdeas.hook: Everyone wants to lead the Ummah but nobody wants to be trustworthy when no one's watching.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your leadership post on Al-Qawi wal-Ameen (DTauCL6jJ8Z) got strong likes-per-view (58 likes / 508 views) — your audience rewards Prophetic leadership content, but you post it rarely. This is a clear gap: you lean political, not leadership, despite it being a core pillar. Framing it as a callout matches what performs for you.
videoIdeas.script: Everyone wants to lead the Ummah. Nobody wants to be trustworthy when no one's watching. The Prophetic model of leadership is two words — Al-Qawi wal-Ameen. Competent and trustworthy. Notice the order isn't influence first. It's not followers first. It's not who has the loudest platform. Most of you have the competence part backwards too — you think leadership is talking. It's carrying weight other people don't want to carry. So before you ask why nobody follows you, ask yourself: are you actually good at the thing? And can people trust you with something small? Because if the answer's no, you don't have a leadership problem. You have a character problem.

visuals.setting: Indoor, calmer setting — bookshelf or plain wall, seated or standing still, lower and more deliberate energy than the public speaking one. Muted tones.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'Al-Qawi wal-Ameen' typed out word by word while you hold a steady close-up stare before the first line lands.
otherHookIdeas: Open on the phrase 'character problem' as text, then rewind to explain how you got there
Prop: place a heavy book or object down on the table on 'carrying weight'
Two-word on-screen labels flashing: COMPETENT / TRUSTWORTHY as you say each

videoIdeas.title: Stop mistaking being loud for being a leader
videoIdeas.hook: Being the loudest person in the group chat is not leadership. It's noise with confidence.
videoIdeas.rationale: Dinoo's 'staying quiet feels safe' framing and saffana's blunt correction format are both performing. You have the same blunt instinct in your captions ('show me how dumb you can be') but you aim it at politics. Redirecting that edge at a self-development lesson fills your leadership pillar while keeping your signature bite.
videoIdeas.script: Being the loudest person in the group chat is not leadership. It's noise with confidence. There's a difference between influence and volume, and most of you can't tell them apart. The brother who talks the most in the room is usually the one who's read the least. Real authority is quiet — it's the person everyone actually turns to when things go wrong, not the one performing when things are fine. Ask yourself honestly: when there's a real problem, does anyone come to you? Or do you just have opinions? Because opinions are cheap. Everybody's got them. The people who lead are the ones who show up and do the boring, unglamorous work while the loud ones are still talking about it.

visuals.setting: Same edgy energy as your political posts — that's your strongest register. Standing, direct, slightly confrontational framing, tight on the face.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open on the punchline 'noise with confidence' as bold on-screen text over a half-second of you shaking your head before the line.
otherHookIdeas: Pattern interrupt: mimic someone rambling for 2 seconds, then cut sharply to you deadpan
On-screen text 'Opinions are cheap' held on the beat
Cut from a chaotic loud clip to total silence on your face

videoIdeas.title: Your low attention span is a character issue
videoIdeas.hook: You don't have a focus problem. You have a discipline problem you've rebranded as ADHD.
videoIdeas.rationale: Mindset is a named pillar but barely represented in your top posts. Doctordaanish's '20s advice, save this' listicle format is doing big numbers right now, and blunt reframes travel far. This is a saveable, shareable mindset take that will provoke comments — your zero-comment videos need debate-bait.
videoIdeas.script: You don't have a focus problem. You have a discipline problem you've rebranded as a personality trait. I'm not saying nobody genuinely struggles — some do. But most of you can watch a two-hour film no problem, yet can't read ten pages without reaching for your phone. That's not your brain being broken. That's your brain being trained. Every time you pick up your phone the second you feel bored, you're teaching yourself that discomfort is an emergency. It isn't. Sit with the boredom. Finish the boring task. Your ability to do hard, dull things when you don't feel like it — that's the whole game. Everyone wants the discipline of the people they admire. Nobody wants the boredom that built it.

visuals.setting: Neutral indoor, seated at a desk with a book and phone in frame. Calm, matter-of-fact, older-brother-across-the-table energy.
visuals.visualHook: Visibly place your phone screen-down and slide it out of frame, then look up — on-screen text: 'It's not ADHD. Read this.'
otherHookIdeas: On-screen text punchline first: 'You rebranded laziness' then explain
Cold open: hold up a book, then look at camera deadpan
Split-second clip of scrolling, then hard cut to stillness

videoIdeas.title: Third spaces are the most important thing our generation is building
videoIdeas.hook: While everyone argues online, young Muslims are quietly building the thing that actually matters.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your third-spaces post (Dbwq4JosFxD) hit 879 views and 64 likes — you clearly have a constructive, community-building angle that resonates but you use it rarely, defaulting to refutations. This is the positive-leadership counterweight your feed lacks, and community content builds a loyal following better than pure conflict content.
videoIdeas.script: While everyone's busy arguing online, young Muslims are quietly building the thing that actually matters. Cafés. Study circles. Community hubs. Spaces where people can meet, learn, and just belong. And of course, some of you can't help but sneer at it — too casual, not serious enough, not Islamic enough. Here's what you're missing: a generation that grew up isolated is teaching itself how to be a community again. That's leadership. Not the loud kind. The kind that builds something real and leaves a door open for the person behind you. If you spent half the energy you use criticising on building — imagine what we'd have. Stop waiting for permission. Build the room you wish existed.

visuals.setting: Filmed in or outside an actual café / community space if possible — warm, populated, real. Walking-and-talking or leaning against a wall, relaxed but purposeful.
visuals.visualHook: B-roll of a busy community space / people talking over coffee for 2 seconds with on-screen text 'This is more important than your online argument.'
otherHookIdeas: Cold open walking into the space, then turn to camera
On-screen text 'Build the room you wish existed' held at the end
Contrast cut: a screen full of arguing comments, then cut to real people in a room

videoIdeas.title: The people criticising everything have built nothing
videoIdeas.hook: Notice how the people with the most criticism have built the least.
videoIdeas.rationale: This channels the exact energy of your best-performing posts (the protest post at 6134 views, the 'spew your venom' post at 109 likes) but pivots it from politics into a universal mindset lesson — so it keeps your signature edge while broadening reach beyond your niche political audience. It's a debate-starter, which fixes your zero-comment problem.
videoIdeas.script: Notice how the people with the most criticism have built the least. It's always the person who's never run anything who has the most opinions on how you should run it. The one who's never spoken in front of anyone telling you your delivery's off. Criticism is free. It costs nothing, it risks nothing, and it makes you feel productive while you sit still. Building is the opposite — it's slow, it's public, and it exposes you. That's why most people choose to comment instead of create. I'm not saying ignore all feedback. I'm saying weigh it by the source. When someone who's actually done the thing corrects you, listen. When someone who's done nothing does — keep building. Their noise is the tax you pay for doing something.

visuals.setting: Your strongest confrontational register — direct to camera, plain background, sharp energy. This is your bread and butter.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'The loudest critics have built nothing' over a hard cut to your face mid-eye-roll.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open on 'Criticism is free' as the punchline, then rewind
Pattern interrupt: read out a fake nasty comment, then respond to camera
On-screen text held at close: 'Their noise is the tax'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post by a mile — 6134 views, 211 likes, a 3.4% like rate. The opener 'Can't believe we're still discussing the necessity of protests in 2026' works because it's a dated, timely, confrontational hook that assumes shared frustration with the viewer — that's your strongest register. Topical urgency plus your blunt voice is clearly what your current audience shows up for.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Almost all your reach comes from political/current-affairs content, which means you're building a commentary audience, not a self-development one — none of your three actual pillars are represented in your top post. Milk this reach: pin a comment or add a CTA that bridges to your leadership/mindset content so these viewers have a reason to follow you for more than the next hot take.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: The subject is spot-on for your public speaking pillar and the observation 'the amount of people that struggle to string a sentence together is shocking' is a genuinely strong, blunt hook line — it's the kind of take that should travel.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 617 views and 0 comments tells you the delivery or hook execution fell flat, not the idea. The caption drifts into 'back in the days people would go outside' nostalgia, which weakens the edge. Cut straight to the reader's problem, give one concrete action ('speak to one stranger a day'), and end on a challenge so people reply. This exact idea is worth re-filming with a sharper hook — see the reworked script above.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 884 views shows the topic held attention, and the distinction you're drawing — trivialising vs. making things fun, leisure vs. work — is a genuinely nuanced take that suits your articulate side.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 0 comments on 884 views is a red flag: the video informs but doesn't provoke a response. The caption opens on 'There is a clear difference between...' which is a lecture opener, not a hook. Lead with the accusation or the stakes, not the framework. And you reference 'I've already spoken about this' — don't assume viewers saw the last one; each video needs to stand alone with its own hook.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 58 likes on 508 views is your best engagement rate in the whole set (11.4%) — your audience clearly rewards concise Prophetic leadership content. 'We often chase influence before character. The Prophetic model reverses that' is exactly your pillar and exactly your voice: tight, quotable, no filler.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This got far fewer views than your political posts despite better engagement, which means the algorithm isn't pushing it and you're not making enough of it. You're underposting your single best-performing pillar. Post leadership content like this weekly, not occasionally, and open with the punchline ('Integrity comes first') rather than the setup to hook faster.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 109 likes on 1045 views — a 10.4% like rate, one of your highest. The rhetorical, confrontational caption ('Does it not ashame you... Is it not time to focus on what's dire?') generates strong agreement-based engagement. Your audience responds to righteous directness.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: This is pure conflict/callout content with no takeaway — it rallies the people who already agree but gives no one a reason to save, share, or follow for future value. Your feed is heavy on this register. Keep the edge but occasionally redirect that same energy toward a constructive lesson (leadership, discipline, speaking) so the anger converts into an audience that sticks, not just a reaction.
